Chevrier, Apodemus chevrieri, a small murid rodent inhabiting the montane forests of southwestern China, exhibits a life history strategy that reflects its seasonal environment. Field studies indicate that neonatal individuals enter the world at a modest mass, with newly born pups weighing approximately 2.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.5 grams]. This low birth weight, characteristic of altricial murids, necessitates an extended period of maternal investment before the offspring achieve nutritional independence. Data derived from laboratory colonies, maintained under controlled thermal conditions, reveal that the weaning process concludes roughly 17 days after birth [tx = roughly 17 days after birth] at a temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This relatively brief pre-weaning phase is comparable to that observed in the closely related wood mouse, Apodemus sylvaticus, from which several life-history estimates for Chevrier have been extrapolated due to the paucity of direct field data. The modest neonatal mass stands in stark contrast to the ultimate size achieved by adult females, which can attain a maximum body mass of 43 grams [Wwi = 43 grams] under favorable resource conditions, though individual variation spanning from 28 to 43 grams is commonly reported across different elevations.

Reproductive timing in Apodemus chevrieri follows a compressed schedule typical of small rodents that must complete breeding cycles within a narrow seasonal window. Gestation, the period of in utero embryonic development, lasts approximately 24 days [tg = approximately 24 days] under standard laboratory conditions maintained near 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C]. This duration aligns closely with estimates for other temperate Apodemus species. Following parturition, the altricial neonates progress through a predictable developmental sequence. The attainment of sexual maturity, marked by the onset of gametogenesis and reproductive activation, occurs at approximately 71 days after birth [tp = approximately 71 days after birth] at a temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This age at puberty, measured in captive individuals housed at a stable temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], suggests that individuals born early in the breeding season could potentially reproduce within the same calendar year, provided that somatic growth has progressed sufficiently to support the energetic demands of gestation and lactation.

Females typically produce litters ranging from one to three pups [N_R_i = litters ranging from one to three pups], a modest fecundity that is nonetheless typical for a rodent of this body mass. Under the ambient thermal conditions of a laboratory set to 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], the maximum reproductive rate equates to approximately 3.5 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 3.5 litters per year]. This annual frequency reflects the combined constraints of a relatively short gestation period and the need to wean each litter before initiating the next pregnancy. The interplay between litter size and frequency suggests that a single female could theoretically produce upwards of nine offspring annually under optimal conditions, though natural populations likely experience lower realized fecundity due to resource limitation, predation pressure, and the energetic costs of lactation during the cooler montane spring.

Metabolic rate represents a fundamental axis of physiological variation that underpins the life-history traits of Apodemus chevrieri. Respirometry trials conducted on adults under standard basal conditions reveal a maximum oxygen consumption rate of 55.4 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 55.4 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This relatively high metabolic demand, typical of small endotherms with elevated surface-area-to-volume ratios, necessitates a correspondingly high food intake rate to sustain both maintenance and reproductive effort. The energetic cost of maintaining a stable core temperature is particularly acute for this species given its montane habitat, where nocturnal ambient temperatures can fall well below the thermoneutral zone. The observed basal metabolic rate is consistent with predictions for a rodent of approximately 43 grams and underscores the physiological challenge of balancing the energetic demands of thermoregulation, somatic growth, and the provision of milk to a rapidly developing litter during the brief summer months.

Longevity records for Apodemus chevrieri remain sparse, but extrapolation from the well-documented demography of Apodemus sylvaticus provides a useful benchmark. A maximum lifespan of approximately 6.3 years [am = approximately 6.3 years] has been inferred for captive individuals maintained at a stable body temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], representing the upper bound of physiological longevity under protected conditions free from predation and resource limitation. This lifespan is considerable for a murid rodent of this size and suggests a relatively slow pace of senescence compared to many temperate mice. Wild populations, however, likely experience substantially reduced longevity due to extrinsic mortality factors. The extended life span, when considered alongside the relatively modest annual reproductive output of approximately 3.5 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 3.5 litters per year], suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes survival across multiple breeding seasons, a pattern that may be adaptive in the unpredictable montane environments where this species has evolved.
